studies.title: The Word became flesh
studies.passage: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life; and the life was the light of men. And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not. … And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
studies.context: John opens with Genesis language. The Word is before creation, is with the Father, is God, and truly enters human life.
studies.orthodox: The Church confesses Jesus Christ as fully divine and fully human. The incarnation is not an appearance or a temporary disguise: God the Son takes on our humanity to heal and unite it to himself.
studies.practice: Pray slowly: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me.’ Notice that the one you address is both the eternal Word and the one who dwelt among us.
questions: What does John say about the Word before creation?
Why does ‘made flesh’ matter for how God meets human suffering?

quiz.prompt: Which claim does John 1 make about the Word?
choices: The Word was with God and was God
The Word was only a prophet

studies.title: The blessed life
studies.passage: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted. Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth. Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.
studies.context: Jesus begins the Sermon on the Mount by naming those whom the kingdom calls blessed, even when the world sees weakness.
studies.orthodox: The Beatitudes are a portrait of life in Christ, not a checklist for earning God's love. Poverty of spirit means humility before God; hungering for righteousness means seeking a life made right by his grace.
studies.practice: Choose one Beatitude. In your evening prayer, name one place where you resisted it and one small way to practice it tomorrow.
questions: Where do you confuse blessing with comfort or status?
What might meekness look like in one tense conversation?

quiz.prompt: What is promised to those who hunger and thirst after righteousness?
In an Orthodox reading, the Beatitudes describe…
choices: A way of life in Christ

studies.title: The Father runs to meet us
studies.passage: And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him. And the son said unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight, and am no more worthy to be called thy son. But the father said to his servants, Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet: And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry: For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry.
studies.context: The younger son turns back after wasting his inheritance. The father sees him before he reaches home and receives him with joy.
studies.orthodox: Repentance is a return to the Father, not a way to make ourselves worthy before we approach him. The Church reads this parable in preparation for Great Lent: confession and mercy belong together.
studies.practice: Begin a prayer with honest confession, then finish it with the father's welcome in mind. If needed, speak with your priest about confession.
questions: What does the father do before the son finishes his speech?
What keeps you from turning toward God when you have failed?

quiz.prompt: Who moves toward the returning son?
choices: The father, who runs to meet him

quiz.prompt: What does repentance mean in this parable?

studies.title: Faith that becomes visible
studies.passage: Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone. Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.
studies.context: James challenges a merely verbal claim to faith when a brother or sister lacks food or clothing.
studies.orthodox: Faith is living trust expressed through love. Good works are not a purchase price for salvation; they are the fruit of cooperating with God's grace and caring for the neighbor before us.
studies.practice: Do one specific act of mercy this week without using it as proof of your worth. Pray for the person as well.
questions: What concrete need does James place near this teaching?
Where can your faith take the shape of service this week?

quiz.prompt: According to James, faith without works is…
How does the Orthodox tradition understand acts of mercy?
choices: A fruit of living faith and grace

studies.title: If Christ be risen
studies.passage: But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept. For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.
studies.context: Paul responds to those denying the resurrection of the dead. He anchors Christian hope in Christ's own rising.
studies.orthodox: Pascha proclaims the defeat of death in the risen Christ. Resurrection is not merely a metaphor for optimism; it is the ground of the Church's worship and hope for the renewal of creation.
studies.practice: Pray the Paschal greeting: ‘Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down death by death.’ Bring one fear of death or loss into that prayer.
questions: How would your week change if resurrection were more than an idea?

quiz.prompt: What does Paul call the risen Christ?
What is at the center of Pascha?

studies.title: A clean heart
studies.passage: Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me. Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit.
studies.context: Psalm 51 in most English Bibles is Psalm 50 in the Greek Septuagint numbering used in Orthodox worship. It is a prayer of repentance and restoration.
studies.orthodox: The psalm asks God to remake the heart. Orthodox prayer repeatedly returns to repentance as healing: we bring our wounds to God rather than pretending we can repair ourselves alone.
studies.practice: Read Psalm 50(51) slowly. Pause after ‘Create in me a clean heart’ and name what you need God to renew.
questions: Why does the psalm ask God to create, not merely polish, a clean heart?
What would restored joy look like in your prayer?

quiz.prompt: Why are two psalm numbers shown?
choices: The Septuagint and common English numbering differ

quiz.prompt: What does the psalmist ask God to renew?
